source.title: Toward Safer Diffusion Language Models: Discovery and Mitigation of Priming Vulnerability

record.file_problem: The full paper text, including appendices, is present. The text identifies the published version as ICLR 2026.
record.tranche_reason: It tests whether token injection and prompt optimization can bypass safety, using denoising-state interventions and suffix attacks on masked diffusion language models rather than the original studies’ autoregressive-model methods.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own jailbreak outcomes for diffusion language models, including intermediate-state token injection, First-Step GCG, and recovery-alignment comparisons. It does not report per-token KL divergence, fine-tuning on a few harmful or benign examples to measure safety erosion, or parameter-localization measurements. Values cited from prior work are not recorded as results.
record.test_reason: The study brings the shallow-alignment questions to masked diffusion LMs, a new setting. Injecting harmful-response tokens into intermediate denoising states is the diffusion analogue of prefilling, and First-Step GCG is a suffix attack; both bear on V4 for the safety-aligned LLaDA Instruct and LLaDA 1.5. Recovery Alignment trains the model to return to safety from contaminated states, the analogue of Qi et al.'s recovery augmentation, so it bears on V7. The RA-without-intervention ablation isolates training-state coverage as the cause, which bears on V6. There is no fine-tuning attack, no per-token KL and no parameter localization.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. To add: the authors attribute the vulnerability to MDLM alignment training only from fully masked starts. They report that RA mitigates it with negligible capability cost and also improves robustness to conventional jailbreaks, though strong attacks (e.g., ReNeLLM) and very late interventions still succeed.
record.recipe_differences: Studies masked diffusion language models rather than the autoregressive models in the cited sources. Uses denoising-state injection and First-Step GCG to test bypass, then trains with reward-model-based Recovery Alignment; it does not use the original fine-tuning or per-token KL measurement recipes.
record.method_sensitivity: ASR changes with the intervention step: the paper reports higher ASR at later steps. Recovery Alignment robustness varies by model and attack; the paper also reports effects of intervention scheduling and generation length in appendices.

fits_no_version.finding: Inserting affirmative or some neutral tokens (e.g., 'Finally', 'mountain') at L/2 sharply lowers refusal-phrase probability mass; harmful tokens do not. Anchoring at tinter=4 drives relative refusal probability near zero for all three models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In diffusion LMs, tokens untypical of refusals at any position suppress the refusal-phrase distribution.

record.problems: Experiments focus on three masked diffusion models and principally report JBB-Behaviors; additional AdvBench experiments use 50 selected prompts. Some refusal-probability results are figure-only. ASR depends on automatic evaluators, and the paper notes that very late interventions can make safe generation difficult and that strong attacks can still bypass Recovery Alignment.
record.rows_left_out: At the 60-row limit, left out Table 2 results for SFT, DPO, MOSA, and other RA ablations across conditions; the additional guardrail and keyword-matching tables; conventional conversational-jailbreak rows; detailed AdvBench results; and further generation-length and intervention-scheduling sweeps. These appear in Tables 2-8 and Figures 3, 9, and Appendix C. They were omitted after retaining the original and full-RA attack conditions, the tinter=4 ablation comparisons, and refusal-probability evidence.

untested.parts: No fine-tuning on harmful examples to remove safety.
No per-token KL between aligned and base models, and no positional analysis of the alignment difference.
No autoregressive models, no prefilling of the literal response opening, no decoding-parameter changes.
No test of whether safety sits in a few weights or ranks. LoRA is used only for training.
The autoregressive argument (alignment objective concentrated on first tokens) is not tested. Only the diffusion analogue is tested: training only from fully masked starts.
No measure of whether safety is spread across response positions, and no test of robustness to harmful fine-tuning after RA.

missing.what: SFT, DPO and MOSA baselines under all attacks. Standard alignment leaves the priming vulnerability (e.g., MOSA tinter=4 ASR 24.0 on LLaDA); this is evidence for V6.
Conventional jailbreaks (PAIR, ReNeLLM, Crescendo) on original vs RA models, including the ReNeLLM non-improvement on MMaDA.
General capability on 11 benchmarks for original, RA w/o inter and RA (averages roughly unchanged; HumanEval and PIQA drop).
Ablations on max intervention step and scheduling (constant scheduling fails; large tmax causes reward hacking).
Monte Carlo GCG vs First-Step GCG ASR (e.g., 20.0 vs 58.0 on LLaDA).
Generation length: at L=512 the original models show raised ASR even with no injection; RA models become more vulnerable as the intervention covers a larger fraction of short outputs.
Judge sensitivity: LlamaGuard and keyword-matching ASR, and AdvBench (50 prompts) results.

record.verdict_notes: The setting is masked diffusion LMs, so the 'opening' of V4 becomes injection at intermediate denoising states, with tokens at random positions rather than a prefix. MMaDA is unaligned (79.7% no-attack ASR), so its original-model rows cannot test bypass of safety, and its RA rows mix basic alignment with deepening. Section 4.1 text (2% to 21%) disagrees with Table 2 (17.3) for LLaDA at tinter=1. The ablation baseline in r55-r57 is the original model; the V6 comparison is against the RA rows r30/r39/r48, now linked.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test whether fine-tuning on a few to a few hundred harmful examples causes a safety-trained chat model to comply.
Does not test whether ordinary or carefully selected benign fine-tuning data increases harmful compliance.
Does not measure per-token KL divergence between aligned and base models or its distribution across response positions.
Tests denoising-state token injection, optimization-based prompt suffixes, and conversational jailbreaks, but not autoregressive compliant-prefix prefilling or decoding changes.
Does not test whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety behavior. LoRA is used for training, not as a localization test.

Tests contaminated-state training as a proposed explanation and mitigation for this diffusion-model vulnerability; does not test the original claim about data or objectives producing first-token concentration in autoregressive models.
Tests recovery alignment and its robustness under the reported attacks, but does not measure whether safety behavior is distributed across response-token positions.

labels.label: supports
labels.condition: Safety-aligned LLaDA Instruct and LLaDA 1.5, JBB-Behaviors, GPT-4o judge, 4 or more injected tokens, PAD, DiJA, First-Step GCG
labels.reason: Table 2 shows substantial bypass from 1–2% unattacked ASR: anchoring reaches 35.0–96.7%, PAD 61.7–67.3%, DiJA 89.7–92.0%, and First-Step GCG 49.5–58.0%.

labels.label: limits_scope
labels.condition: Minimal injection (one token, tinter=1) in diffusion LMs
labels.reason: Table 2 gives 17.3% and 14.7% ASR for one-token anchoring, substantially below larger interventions; Section C.1 confirms random token selection by masking.

labels.label: supports
labels.condition: MDLMs aligned only from fully masked starts vs RA trained from contaminated states, anchoring tinter=4
labels.reason: With the RA objective retained, omitting intermediate-state training yields 22.0%, 27.7%, and 25.3% ASR versus 1.3%, 0.7%, and 13.0% with RA, supporting a causal contribution from training-state coverage.

labels.label: supports
labels.condition: RA on LLaDA Instruct and LLaDA 1.5, anchoring tinter up to 16, and PAD
labels.reason: Table 2 shows anchoring ASR reduced to 0–8.3% through tinter=16 and PAD ASR to 1.0%; unattacked ASR is 0.0% for both RA models.

labels.label: limits_scope
labels.condition: Very late injection (tinter=32), DiJA, First-Step GCG, and RA on the unaligned MMaDA
labels.reason: Table 2 retains 43.0–79.3% ASR at tinter=32, 35.7–70.0% under DiJA, and 11.3–45.7% under First-Step GCG; MMaDA also retains 34.3% at tinter=16 and 24.3% under PAD.

labels.label: limits_scope
labels.condition: Conventional jailbreaks (ReNeLLM) and capability cost; text-based, no rows
labels.reason: Table 3 leaves LLaDA ReNeLLM ASR at 72.3% and raises MMaDA from 79.3% to 81.7%. Table 4 lowers LLaDA HumanEval from 22.0% to 17.1% and PIQA from 74.4% to 71.6%.

relation.reason: Reports its own attack-success measurements, mitigation experiments, and a training-state ablation bearing on V4, V6, and V7.

tranche.reason: Tests bypass, training-state coverage, and safety recovery in masked diffusion language models, a new architectural setting relative to the autoregressive originals.

source_check.notes: Section 4.1 reports 21% LLaDA one-token ASR, whereas Table 2 reports 17.3 ± 4.6%; the checked rows correctly use Table 2. Diffusion priming and recovery support architectural analogues, without directly testing autoregressive first-response-token concentration.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Original models under denoising-state injection, PAD/DiJA, and First-Step GCG on JBB-Behaviors
reader_labels.reason: Attack success rises substantially over unattacked conditions for the original models; first-step GCG also succeeds. See r02-r09, r11-r18, r20-r27, and refusal-probability results r58-r60.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Recovery-Aligned models and MMaDA under the reported attacks
reader_labels.reason: Recovery Alignment substantially lowers attack success, though residual ASR remains for late interventions and several attacks; MMaDA also starts with high no-attack ASR. See r19-r27 and r28-r54.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: RA without contaminated-state training versus original models under anchoring at tinter=4
reader_labels.reason: The no-intervention ablation retains higher ASR than the full recovery-alignment method at this attack setting, consistent with the paper's claim that training from contaminated states matters. See r30, r39, r48, and ablation rows r55-r57.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Recovery Alignment across tested models and denoising-state attacks
reader_labels.reason: Training on contaminated intermediate states lowers ASR relative to original checkpoints across the reported model and attack conditions. See r29-r54.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Late interventions, DiJA, First-Step GCG, and MMaDA under Recovery Alignment
reader_labels.reason: Recovery Alignment leaves substantial residual ASR in some settings; the authors also report that very late interventions challenge safe recovery. See r33, r35-r36, r42, r44-r45, and r50-r54.
